repos.title: LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation
repos.paper_summary:
LightRAG is a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation system. An LLM extracts entities and relations from chunks of size 1200, profiles each as a key-value pair, and deduplicates the resulting graph. At query time, local keywords match entities and global keywords match relations, and one-hop neighbors of the matches are added as context for a general LLM. New documents are indexed by merging their subgraphs into the existing graph instead of rebuilding it.

The evaluation uses four UltraDomain datasets (Agriculture, CS, Legal, Mix), with 125 generated questions per dataset, GPT-4o-mini as the default LLM, and pairwise LLM judgments reported as win rates. Against NaiveRAG on Legal, LightRAG wins 84.8% overall. Against GraphRAG, the margins are small: overall win rates of 54.8% on Agriculture, 52.0% on CS, 52.8% on Legal, and 49.6% on Mix.

The judgments come from a single LLM judge, not human or ground-truth labels. The ablation and cost results are cut off in the provided text, so this summary does not report them.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing RAG systems rely on flat representations and produce fragmented answers, so the paper proposes graph-based indexing with incremental updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
digest_headlines.headline: The paper formalizes RAG as indexing and retrieval followed by generation, and sets three design goals for an efficient system.

digest_headlines.heading: The LightRAG Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG builds a knowledge graph with LLM extraction, updates it incrementally, and retrieves through dual-level keyword matching.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG wins LLM-judged comparisons against four baselines on UltraDomain datasets, and uses far fewer retrieval tokens than GraphRAG.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work finds graph-based RAG lacks dynamic updates, and surveys three ways LLMs are combined with graph data.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: LightRAG is concluded to improve retrieval speed and quality and cut LLM inference costs through graph indexing and incremental updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, a case study against NaiveRAG, and the prompts for graph generation, query generation, keyword extraction and evaluation.

repos.title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction
repos.paper_summary: Edge0 is a streaming inference engine for 35B-class mixture-of-experts models on a 24 GB consumer machine. Expert weights stay on SSD and are memory-mapped on demand, so peak memory tracks the active experts, not all parameters. A per-layer prerouter head predicts the next layer's routing one token ahead, so expert reads overlap the current forward pass. The prediction is used as the routing itself, so the staged experts match the routed experts and none are dropped. An unmerged int4 recovery LoRA, distilled from the fp16 teacher on the student routing path, recovers quality lost to quantization and routing replacement. On a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB, the 35B tier decodes at 20.4 tok/s with 2.9 GiB peak active memory, and the 8B tier at 28.0 tok/s with 1.5 GiB. On OpenCompass, the 35B tier averages 79.2 against 83.2 for its fp16 base, and the 8B tier 69.9 against 72.7. Limitations: AIME loses 6.1 points (35B) and 10.0 points (8B), requests are served one at a time, and CPU graph building sets a 44 ms per-step floor.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Storing 35B-class MoE weights on a 24 GB machine is the bottleneck, so Edge0 keeps experts on SSD and streams them.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior offloading moves the weight footprint rather than shrinking it, and pre-gating schedules next-block experts too late for a streaming engine.

digest_headlines.heading: System Design
digest_headlines.headline: A 40-layer MoE needs 16.9 GiB of routed experts, so Edge0 mmaps them from SSD across four executor paths.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Three training phases make the model work under replaced routing: head distillation, fine-tuning on the student path, and on-policy distillation.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Both tiers average within a few points of fp16 bases, and the prerouter adds +80 to +84% decode where weights do not fit.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Decode has a 44 ms per-step floor from graph building, quality loss concentrates in long-chain reasoning, and one backend exists.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A 35B MoE runs at 20 tok/s in 3 GiB on a 24 GB desktop, with framework, checkpoints, and adapters open source.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the softmax-top-k and sigmoid-group routing formulas and the incremental-stack assembly A/B results.

repos.title: EvoMemState: Evolving Memory State for Personal Agents
repos.paper_summary: EvoMemState is a memory framework for LLM personal agents. It keeps each fact with Relational States (its validity, scope, and links such as `SUPERSEDES` and `CONFLICTS_WITH`) and generates a request-specific Reasoning State describing how retrieved facts apply. A GRPO-trained policy produces Reasoning States, with rewards equal to the frozen agent's score with the state minus its score without it, so training needs reference answers. At inference, the system retrieves K similar facts and expands them through memory relations. On MemSyco-Bench, MemTrapBench, LoCoMo, and LoCoMo-Refined, compared with nine memory systems, it reaches an overall average of 59.9 with Qwen3-8B (best baseline 53.6, SimpleMem) and 61.2 with GPT-4o-mini (best baseline 54.2, MemoryBank). Gains are not uniform: with Qwen3-8B, its CogBias accuracy is 62.3, below LightMem's 69.9. The paper states that it covers text-only histories; multimodal memory is future work. The provided text is truncated before the baseline descriptions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fact-centric memory systems miss how facts update and conflict, motivating a state-centric framework with three components.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminary Studies
digest_headlines.headline: Preliminary studies find related memories are often not retrieved together, and full retrieval does not ensure correct use.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Method builds an ontology of facts, trains a policy to generate Reasoning States, and reasons over both states.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiment
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments show gains over nine baselines on memory-use and dialogue benchmarks, with each component contributing in ablations.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers personal user modeling and long-term memory systems that maintain and organize user information.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion states that reliable personal memory needs both coherent state construction and use-driven state evolution.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitation
digest_headlines.headline: The method handles only text histories, leaving multimodal personal information such as documents and images for future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Use of Large Language Models
digest_headlines.headline: Authors disclose that large language models were used for English editing and table formatting, with authors reviewing all output.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists frequently asked questions, method details, prompts, extended related work, and figures for case studies and efficiency.

repos.title: Fast and Accurate Hand Estimation in Pixels, Interaction and World Space
repos.paper_summary: FAH is a family of hand-pose models built on SAM 3D Body's hand branch. The method predicts corresponding 2D and 3D hand joints and surface points with a heatmap head, then fits MANO or MHR-Hand meshes in a separate stage. Optional heads estimate anatomical parts and contact without object geometry at inference, a causal refiner smooths video tracks, and a camera model places hands in world space. In a controlled comparison within one network, directly predicted 3D points gave better mesh accuracy than predicting MANO parameters. On HOT3D v1, FAH-L reaches 4.31 mm PA-MPJPE and 8.89 mm root error at 65 fps with mesh fitting on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, against 6.72 mm PA for WiLoR and 9.46 mm PA for HaMeR (4.6 fps). The smallest model, FAH-S, runs at 101 fps. The paper names camera estimation as the main source of world-space error, and states that contact without object geometry remains ambiguous, with most contact vertices hidden on 96% of HOT3D contact hands.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Rig-based hand estimators propagate articulation errors to 2D landmarks, so FAH predicts points and fits meshes separately.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work regresses mesh parameters or vertices, and some contact methods need object shape and pose.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: FAH distills SAM 3D Body's hand branch into ViT students and predicts dense 2D and 3D points with a heatmap head.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the egocentric benchmark, the default FAH model's aligned joint error is 4.31 mm, below WiLoR's 6.72 mm.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Camera estimation dominates world-space error, and contact remains ambiguous without object geometry.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training sources, teacher and student settings, label conventions, and image credits.

repos.title: SubRoformer: Subband Time-Domain Representation for Music Source Separation
repos.paper_summary: SubRoFormer is a Transformer-based music source separation system that splits a stereo mix into frequency-localized subbands, runs a separator on temporally compressed features, and predicts complex masks at 100 Hz. The subband module uses an overlapping triangular FIR filter bank, complex analytic conversion, baseband demodulation, and decimation, with a fast polyphase implementation. The separator combines a patched axial RoFormer (alternating subband-axis and temporal-axis attention with rotary embeddings) with a GEGLU gated residual fusion that merges coarse and fine-rate features. On MUSDB18-HQ, training only on that dataset, the target-specific models reach an average SDR of 10.63 dB across four stems, 0.61 dB above the strongest complete public-data BS-RoFormer result the authors report, and 0.99 dB above the reported Mel-RoFormer result. BS-RoFormer is 1.38 dB better on bass. With 500 extra training songs, a single multi-stem model reaches 11.59 dB. The subband transform alone reconstructs the mixture at 27.8 dB SDR-scale fidelity for mel and ERB banks, far below the near-perfect STFT and MDCT controls. The authors state the results are single-seed and directional, and that repeated seeds, efficiency measurements, and parameter-matched ablations are still needed.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Subband frontend plus a residual RoFormer separator targets the time-frequency trade-off in music source separation.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior systems span waveform, hybrid, spectrogram, and subband separators, and the paper positions itself among them.

digest_headlines.heading: Subband Time-Domain Representation
digest_headlines.headline: A fixed triangular subband filter bank with polyphase implementation reconstructs the mixture with measured distortion.

digest_headlines.heading: Residual SubRoFormer
digest_headlines.headline: SubRoFormer combines fine-rate features, a patched axial RoFormer, and gated residual fusion to predict complex masks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use MUSDB18-HQ with SDR as the primary metric, and training data and augmentation are described.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: SubRoFormer-B reaches 10.63 dB on MUSDB18-HQ without extra data, but the authors call the evidence preliminary.

repos.title: RobotAgentBench: Towards Open-world Robot Autonomy
repos.paper_summary: RobotAgentBench (RAB) is a simulation benchmark for evaluating robot agents on open-world household tasks. An agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline builds 50 layouts in Isaac Sim, with 90 atomic tasks, 18 short-horizon tasks, 8 long-horizon tasks, and 4 open-ended scenarios. Tasks test five capabilities: task discovery, context reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and disturbance handling. Scenarios test end-to-end progress. Eleven standalone VLA/WAM policies and five agent architectures run on the same 22-dimensional command interface, with 30 instances per task or scenario. The best standalone policy, InternVLA-A1.5, averages 18.0 on task-level scores. The best agent, a code planner and verifier that calls both code and learned policies (C/H/C), averages 48.5 and scores 15.4 on open-ended scenarios, versus 2.0 for the best standalone model there. Recursive self-improvement raises the code-only Codex harness from 31.0 to 42.3 on the task-level average. Limitations: all results are simulated, real-world results are described only qualitatively, and open-ended scores remain low.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Current benchmarks test isolated manipulation skills, so this work proposes a benchmark for full robot autonomy in household settings.

digest_headlines.heading: RobotAgentBench
digest_headlines.headline: Real rooms are rebuilt in simulation to create 50 layouts, and five agent architectures are compared under one framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Standalone policies average at most 18.0, while the best agent, a hybrid code and learned-policy design, reaches 48.5.

repos.title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
repos.paper_summary: SpecPilot is an autonomous agentic loop that searches for lossless speculative decoding optimizations tailored to each deployment. A cost model ranks the largest gaps between the current system and an estimated speedup ceiling, parallel agents explore directions on separate GPUs, and a controller promotes only changes with a significant gain on unseen requests. Token forcing checks every output token against the stock engine, catching lossy changes that task accuracy misses. Validated mechanisms are stored in structured memory and reused across rounds and deployments. Discovered mechanisms include W12, a lossless 12-bit weight format averaging 12.01–12.02 bits per weight; best-first tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets; two-level verification using an 8-bit view of W12 as a low-precision pre-check; and three batching mechanisms. Across four target models, three drafters, two GPUs and five benchmarks, speedup over autoregressive (AR) decoding rises from stock's 4.46× to 10.87× with one request, and from 1.94× to 3.93× with batching. On H100 with one request, the paper reports 1.84× faster than DDTree. The gains are reported without training or quality loss. Limitations: the loop depends on agent-driven search, and results are measured only on the listed models, drafters, GPUs and benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Stock parallel-drafter systems leave speedup unrealized, which motivates SpecPilot's per-deployment search.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Lossless speculative decoding accepts only tokens matching the exact target's argmax, so output tests cannot easily verify it.

digest_headlines.heading: SpecPilot
digest_headlines.headline: A cost model finds the largest gap to a ceiling, and a controller accepts changes only on confirmed gains.

digest_headlines.heading: Discovered Lossless Algorithms
digest_headlines.headline: SpecPilot discovered a lossless 12-bit weight format, best-first tree verification, two-level verification and batching mechanisms.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Sealed finals on unseen requests give single-request gains of 2.13× to 2.44× and batching gains of 1.85× to 3.11×.

repos.title: Optimizing the Interface Between Knowledge Graphs and LLMs for Complex Reasoning
repos.paper_summary:
Dreamify is a hyperparameter optimization framework for Cognee, a modular system that constructs knowledge graphs and retrieves context for LLMs. It uses Tree-structured Parzen Estimator to tune six parameters: chunk size, retriever type, top-k count, QA prompt, graph extraction prompt, and task preprocessing method. The authors evaluate on filtered subsets of HotPotQA, TwoWikiMultiHop, and MuSiQue, using 24 training and 12 test instances per dataset. Each experiment runs 50 trials, scoring configurations by exact match, F1, or DeepEval correctness.

Optimization yields consistent gains over default baselines. For example, HotPotQA exact match rises from 0.042 to 0.667, and F1 increases from 0.169 to 0.840. On the held-out test sets, performance generally remains above baseline but drops slightly compared to training scores; however, TwoWikiMultiHop F1 improves from 0.625 in training to 0.704 in testing. The paper notes that small evaluation sets introduce variability, and no single configuration performs best across all benchmarks, indicating that optimal settings are task-specific.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hyperparameter tuning of graph-enhanced retrieval pipelines is underexamined, though many interacting settings affect multi-hop question answering.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers retrieval-augmented pipelines, three multi-hop benchmarks, graph-based question answering, and prior optimization of such pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: Automated Knowledge Graph Construction: Cognee
digest_headlines.headline: Cognee is an open-source framework whose modular pipeline and built-in evaluation let the whole system serve as an optimization objective.

digest_headlines.heading: Hyperparameter Optimization Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Dreamify tunes six Cognee parameters with a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator, scoring each trial by a benchmark metric averaged over questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Nine experiments pair three datasets with three metrics, each running 50 trials on 24 training and 12 test instances per dataset.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Tuned settings beat baselines on all nine training metrics, but most hold-out scores fell below training scores.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Tuning gave consistent but uneven gains, and the authors call for custom benchmarks and better evaluation of graph-based systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix describes Cognee's extract-cognify-load architecture, its default pipeline stages, retriever types, and the evaluation framework.

repos.title: GroundingPI: A Grounding Foundation Model towards Physical Intelligence with Visual Primitives
repos.paper_summary:
GroundingPI is a 4B-parameter grounding foundation model that outputs points and boxes as quantized coordinate tokens in a shared vocabulary. It is trained with multimodal and spatial pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO reinforcement learning. On 34 grounding benchmarks spanning 11 perceptual capabilities, it averages 73.68% against 44 baselines, above GPT-6 Astra at 71.54%. Metrics are F1 with mIoU for boxes and OCR, F1 at point for pointing, and task accuracy otherwise. As a visual backbone in a shared flow-matching action head, it outperforms every evaluated mainstream backbone in four out-of-distribution RoboTwin 2.0 settings, by up to 24.8% relative to the strongest. On RoboCasa-GR1 it reaches baseline-level results with 50% of demonstrations versus 75% for the baselines. On nuScenes trajectory prediction it reaches an open-loop L2 error of 0.296 m. Driving uses a language-token trajectory interface with cross-entropy training.

The paper reports gaps on tiny-box localization, high-IoU boundaries, TotalText OCR, FSC147 visual prompting, and GUI grounding. Baseline prompt and parser incompatibilities limit several comparisons, and the manipulation pretrained backbones differ in scale and supervision. Driving is evaluated open loop only.

digest_headlines.heading: Abstract
digest_headlines.headline: The abstract presents GroundingPI, a grounding foundation model meant to improve perception for robot manipulation and driving.

repos.title: Watch Your Step: Anticipated Perception for Humanoid Locomotion
repos.paper_summary: Watch Your Step introduces a perceptive locomotion framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid in which a lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts the next two footholds from proprioception and the velocity command, and the policy observes only small 7×7 elevation-map patches around those predicted footholds. The FPM is an MLP with two 128-unit hidden layers, trained by Huber regression on labeled footholds from recent policy rollouts and refit every 500 PPO iterations, jointly with a PPO locomotion policy. On the training terrain curriculum, the FPM policy reaches level 5 after 7.5k iterations, against 26.1k for the complete-map baseline (HM) and 20.0k for an attention-based encoder (AME2). AME2 ends slightly higher at 40k iterations but needs four GPUs and 6.3 s per policy update versus 0.55 s. In simulation, the FPM policy achieves 74.2% success on sparse corridor terrain versus 71.7% for AME2 and at most 42.7% for the other baselines, and 77.7% on out-of-distribution gaps. The policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 on stairs, a 0.55 m gap, and a 0.6 m drop. Limitations include reliance on an elevation map and that the policy's cautious behavior near unseen gaps is a hypothesis rather than a measured result.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Predicting footholds from proprioception and filtering the elevation map around them should cut redundant input for perceptive humanoid locomotion.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: The locomotion task is set as a reinforcement learning problem for a 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid trained with PPO in 8192 parallel environments.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A blind foothold predictor is retrained periodically, and the policy sees only small height patches around its two predicted footholds.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments and Results
digest_headlines.headline: The gated policy reaches curriculum level 5 in 7.5k iterations, 3.4 to 3.5 times faster than full-map methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The approach trails full-map methods on stepped corridor terrain and cannot see obstacles approaching from the side.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Sampling the elevation map around predicted footholds learns faster than full-map policies and transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1.
